extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic theology; clergy and advanced readers studying the doctrine of justification
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and defense of the Catholic teaching on justification as defined by the Council of Trent, including its definition, elements, causes, process, and refutation of Protestant (especially Lutheran and Calvinist) errors. Aimed at explaining what constitutes true justification, its necessary components, and its theological consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Justification (Tridentine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification is “a translation from that state wherein man is born a child of the first Adam, to the state of grace and of the adoption of the sons of God through the second Adam, Jesus Christ.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification has both a negative element (forgiveness of sin) and a positive element (interior sanctification through merits of Christ). The two are objectively inseparable but treated separately to refute the Lutheran imputation theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Act vs. State of Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful distinction between justification as an act (actus iustificationis) and as an habitual state (habitus iustificationis / status gratiae sanctificantis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transient justificatory act introduces a permanent state (analogous to sacramental effects like Holy Orders). This distinction shapes theological analysis and pastoral application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification, both as act and as state, possesses three properties: it is uncertain, unequal, and capable of being lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties underlie further divisions of the topic (nature, sanctifying grace, properties) and inform pastoral/theological implications (e.g., possibility of falling from grace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Element: Real Remission (not mere imputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The remission of sins in justification is a real annihilation or blotting out of guilt; sins are truly taken away, not merely 'covered' or non-imputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by multiple Scriptural texts (Ps. L, Is. XLIII, Acts III, etc.) and Patristic testimony; explicitly opposed to Lutheran/Protestant theories that treat forgiveness as only forensic non-imputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive Element: Inherent Sanctifying Grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification is not merely the remission of sins but also the sanctification and renewal of the inward man through the voluntary reception of grace and gifts inherent in the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent anathematizes doctrines that reduce justification to sole imputation or sole remission; theologians call this inherent grace the 'grace of justification' which effects sanctification, adoption, and other formal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fides formata vs. Fides informis (Formed vs. Dead Faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only fides formata (faith animated by charity and productive of good works) truly justifies; fides informis (dead faith devoid of charity) does not justify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tridentine Fathers and Scholastic theology distinguish these to guard against the notion of a faith that is merely intellectual or forensic. The Council condemns assertions that faith without charity is 'true faith.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Process/Stages of Conversion (Tridentine Schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary stages in the process of justification: (1) from faith to fear of divine justice; (2) from fear to hope; (3) from hope to initial love; (4) from initial love to contrition and a firm purpose of amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These preparatory acts (initia fidei) are described psychologically by the Council; faith is the beginning/root but typically precedes and elicits the other acts. The sequence is descriptive, not absolutely rigid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrition as a Condition for Forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrition is a conditio sine qua non for forgiveness; explicit contrition for mortal sins is necessary for justification, though perfect charity may in exceptional cases 'virtually' include intermediate stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sorrow is imperfect (attritio), justification for mortal sins requires actual reception of the Sacrament (Baptism or Penance). St. Thomas and the Tridentine teaching limit virtual penance to venial or forgettable grievous sins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacraments as Instrumental Causes (Baptism and Penance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sacrament of Baptism is the instrumental cause of justification; Baptism (and Penance) truly removes guilt, with Baptism completely removing original sin and effecting regeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural and patristic citations support baptism as a 'laver of regeneration' that both remits sins and confers a lasting state of grace; infant baptism therefore effects justification for infants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctifying Grace as the Sole Formal Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying (inherent) grace is the sole formal cause of justification: it by itself produces the formal effects of justification (forgiveness, sanctification, adoption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent defines this as an article of faith, excluding doctrines that make the formal cause merely an external imputation or mere favor without inherent renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of Causes of Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Council lists the causes: final cause (glory of God and life everlasting), efficient cause (merciful God who washes and sanctifies), meritorious cause (Christ's passion), instrumental cause (Sacrament of Baptism), and sole formal cause (the justice of God by which He makes us just).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multi-causal framework clarifies how divine action, Christ's merits, sacraments, and inherent grace cooperate in justification, and is used to refute reductionist Protestant accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Forensic Imputation as Sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that justification is merely the outward imputation of Christ's righteousness (iustitia Christi extra nos) and leaves the sinner inwardly unchanged is rejected as heretical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual, patristic, and philosophical arguments are marshaled: biblical language of regeneration, patristic unanimity, and moral absurdities (e.g., universal identical sanctity, loss of justification only by unbelief, exclusion of infants) show imputation-alone is untenable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regeneration / New Creation as Integral to Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification effects regeneration and renovation: the sinner becomes a 'new creature,' renewed in spirit, a child of God, and endowed with a new nature (status gratiae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural support (Tit. III, 5; 2 Cor. V, 17; Gal. VI, 15) and patristic testimony (Chrysostom, Ambrose) present justification as an objective inward transformation, not merely declarative status.
